records.title: Aviation Medicine. Monthly Progress Report No. 7.
records.locator: OEMcmr-36:7, human chamber section (NLM item 101085500X267, image 498–500)
records.note: Cumulative Cincinnati study report with repeated chamber flights. The procedure for ending individual exposures changed after the first approximately 75–100 flights. Symptoms and grades follow the historical authors' definitions. The same individual could contribute to multiple conditions. The report does not identify the earlier letter participants or arm-level correspondence to later Cincinnati compilations.

records.title: Summary of Monthly Progress Reports.
records.locator: FLEXNER:1942-11-01, human chamber section (NLM item 101085500X267, image 1)
records.note: The Cincinnati entry repeats the investigator names, contract, 35 participants, 240 ascents and 35,000-ft setting. The extended oxygen statement gives seven people reported protected, without total exposed or arm linkage.

records.title: Aviation Medicine. Bi-Monthly Progress Report No. 19.
records.locator: OEMcmr-36:19, human chamber section (NLM item 101085500X267, image 517–518)
records.note: The authors report 29 new participants, each exposed under six conditions. The 35,000-ft preselection test came first and the five subsequent conditions were randomized. The August report enumerates all six; the October text omits the ground-preparation entry in its numbered list but discusses it in the conclusions. NASA separately cites Cincinnati Report 385.

condition_profiles.activity: Five deep knee bends every three minutes.

records.title: Physiological Factors Conditioning Responses of Mammals to Rapid Decompression and Recompression. Bi-Monthly Progress Report No. 14.
records.locator: OEMcmr-74:14, human chamber section (NLM item 101085500X267, image 752–753)
records.note: October 1943 work on 37 young adult men, matching the three slow and two explosive runs per participant in Fulton 1951 Table 91 Group II. This contemporary report adds repeat-class agreement and summarizes time at altitude. The category margins do not provide new independent clinical events. The printed slow rate in ft/s conflicts with the stated 17-minute ascent. The report describes increased onset time although its means at altitude are shorter.
